1-10 Check-In

Ask students how they are feeling today. “Take a few moments to check-in with yourself and notice how you are feeling. Do you feel good? Bad? Excited? Nervous? Somewhere in the middle? Remember, there is no right or wrong response, as long as you are being truthful.”

Go around the room, asking students to share their number, from 1-10, responding to each student’s number with a neutral/appreciative acknowledgement of any number they choose.

Lesson Purpose

Tell students that today they will learn their first note on the recorder as well as learning how to identify different symbols and markings on sheet music.

Assess Prior Knowledge

Hold up (or display on the projector) the sample sheet music (included). Ask students, “Do any of you already know how to read sheet music? If so, can you point out some of the different symbols you see and tell me what they are named?” Allow 4-6 students to respond. Explain that this class will teach students to read the music, in the same way they can now read books - they just have to learn the meaning of the symbols!

",,,"

If You Can Hear My Voice

“Now it is time to warm up our bodies and voices so that we are prepared to focus, have fun, and make music together.”

Begin every class warm-up with the singing cue, “If you can hear my voice,_____________.” The phrase can be finished with any cue and can be sung on solfège scale degrees, “sol-do-do-do-do-do-do-sol,” or any simple melody of your choice. For example, you might sing, “If you can hear my voice, stand up.” Give them a few cues to get used to this method of listening and following directions. Teachers can use this or another attention-getter during transitions or moments when students need to focus and be attentive during instruction.

Sample cues:

“Stand up”

“Reach up tall”

“Stretch to your toes”

“Shoulders up, shoulders back, shoulders down”

“Wave hello”

“Twist back and forth”

“Sit down”

","

Introduction to Music Notation

Display the sample sheet music (provided) on the board to use as a reference. Explain that music has its own “alphabet“ of symbols that allow musicians to read all the information needed to play a song. This includes when to play, which notes to play, how long to play them, etc.

The symbols are written on a staff, or series of 5 stacked, horizontal lines. Draw a set of 5 horizontal lines on the board, or show a pre-drawn staff on a felt board, and then ask students to see if they can find the staff on the sample sheet music that they have received. For the recorder instrument, we will be playing notes in the treble clef, which you will know by looking at the symbol on the left side of the staff. Write a treble clef on the blank staff on the board, then ask students to find the treble clef symbol on the sample sheet music.

When you place a note on one of these lines, or in the spaces between the lines, that will tell us which note to play. Each note has a different letter name, all the way from letter A to letter G. Draw a whole note on each line and space, with the corresponding note names below.

“Musicians often use silly sentences to help them remember which letters go on each line and space. For example, the notes that are on the spaces of the staff are F, A, C, E -- which spells “face“ and therefore makes those notes easier to remember!” Show an example of notes F, A, C, and E on the staff.

“The notes that are on the lines of the staff are E, G, B, D, and F. Musicians sometimes remember these notes by saying, “Every Good Boy Does Fine.” Show an example of notes E, G, B, D, and F on the staff.

Next, begin with a blank staff and write a B whole note on the middle line of the staff. Ask students to see if they can identify which note this is, using the diagram of notes and corresponding letters. “It is a B!” Explain that this is the first note we are going to learn to play on the recorder!

","

Instrument Distribution

Ask students to sit quietly in their chairs and place their hands folded on top of the desk. Distribute the student’s recorder and music folder by placing each on top of their desk (feel free to designate 2-3 student helpers to assist in passing out instruments and materials). Remind students to wait before touching or playing their instruments or folders until they have been instructed to do so.

Rest, Ready, and Play Positions (Review)

Practice the three positions you will use for the recorder: Rest, Ready, and Play position.

Rest position is where you place the recorder in your lap or on your desk. This position is used when you need students to listen to instructions and you should not hear any playing of instruments.

Ready position is when you place your hands on the recorder, left over right, and bring the instrument in front of your mouth, ready to play. Like Rest position, you should not hear any sound or playing of instruments in Ready position.

Play position is when you gently blow into the mouthpiece to play a note on the recorder. You are seated with a tall back, feet uncrossed and flat on the floor, sitting toward the edge of your seat.

Practice Rest and Ready position until all students respond with consistency and accuracy. There should be no sound coming from the recorder at this time. Then, with everyone seated in Rest position, explain that when you say, “Play position,” students may pick up their instrument and play any note on their recorder. “While you are playing, you will need to keep your eyes on me so you can see the cue to stop playing.” Model the conductor’s hand gesture to stop playing by holding up your open hand and wrapping it into a closed fist.

Cue, “Ready position,” and wait for all students to respond quietly, getting their instrument into the proper position for play. Then cue, “Play position,” and allow them to play a note from 5-10 seconds. Cue them to stop with the conductor’s hand gesture and ask students to return to “Rest position.” Remind students to place the recorder gently on the top of their desks, hands in their lap so as not to be tempted to touch the instrument.

First Note: B

Invite students to place their hand map on the desk in front of them for reference. Write the letter “B” on the board under the whole note you drew on the staff earlier in the lesson. Model the finger position for a B note on the recorder, explaining that this note uses fingers one and two of the top hand, or left hand. This includes the covering of the thumb hole on the back of the recorder with your left thumb, and the top hole on the front of the instrument with your left index fin

Cue students to pick up their instruments in Ready position, ensuring that no sound is being played yet on the instrument, and place their hands on the correct holes to play a B. Explain that when they put the mouthpiece to their mouth, it should rest lightly on the edge of their lips, not touching their teeth or far enough in their mouth that they could bite down on the mouthpiece. Just enough to blow slow, light air into the instrument. On the cue, “Play position,” have students blow into the mouthpiece and play note B for 15-30 seconds. During this time, the teacher should rotate around the room, correcting any finger positions or breathing.

Greatest B

Return to Rest position. Ask students to raise a quiet hand if they think they can play a really soft B note. Select 2-3 students to demonstrate playing a soft B note. Then ask if they think they can play a really long B. Select 2-3 students to demonstrate how long they can play the note, the rest of the class can count aloud, in a whisper voice. Finally, ask who thinks they can play a B with a really good tone, or sound? Select 2-3 students to demonstrate.

","

Collect Materials

Have students return their recorders inside their case and collect all instruments and music folders. If students take the recorders home, instruct them to place them safely in their backpacks or desks. If the instruments stay in the classroom, designate a bin or other storage container to collect the recorders and music folders. Use student helpers to make this clean up process safe and efficient.

Reflection

Ask students, “What is one new thing you learned today that you didn’t know before class?” Invite 3-5 students to share, encouraging a silent shake response from the rest of the class if they are in agreement.

Recorder Wave — stand in “Musicians ready” position, lift your left hand up, lift your right hand, and shake both hands with palms open. As you do the movements, say, “Left” (holding up the left hand), “Right” (hold up the right hand), “Outta sight!” (shaking both hands in silent applause and then quickly placing them behind your back).

Continue on to the bow:

One-Arm Bow — lift one arm up to the ceiling, fold forward bringing your arm down by your ankles, leave both arms down by your side and stand back up tall, returning to “Musicians ready” position.

Spaghetti Bow — lift one arm up toward the ceiling; as you fold forward, spiral your hand in a fancy gesture, as if spinning spaghetti noodles around your hand, and bring the arm across the waist. Then, stand back up, bringing your arm back to the side in “Musicians ready” position.

One-Leg Bow — step one leg out to the side and cross the other leg behind. Bend the standing leg and fold forward in a curtsy bringing either one arm in front of the chest or presenting both arms out wide to the side. Practice on both sides.

Finish with a group round of applause.

Lesson Purpose

Tell students that today they will learn how musicians create their own music and songs and they will even create an original piece of music as a class.

Assess Prior Knowledge

Ask students, “Raise your hand if you know what a ‘composer’ is in music?” Invite students with raised hands to share a definition in their own words. Then explain that a composer is someone who writes music.

If You Can Hear My Voice (Student-Led)

“Now it is time to warm up our bodies and voices so that we are prepared to focus, have fun, and make music together.”

Invite a student from the class to lead the warm-up using the singing cue, “If you can hear my voice, _____________.” The phrase can be finished with any cue and can be sung on solfège scale degrees, “sol-do-do-do-do-do-do-sol,” or any simple melody of your choice. You can select a new student leader for each class. As the student sings the warm-up cues, you as the teacher should follow along with the rest of the class.

Sample cues:

“Stand up”

“Reach up tall”

“Stretch to your toes”

“Shoulders up, shoulders back, shoulders down”

“Wave hello”

“Twist back and forth”

“Sit down”

The Composer

“Now that you have learned many of the notes and rhythms that can be played on the recorder, let’s learn about how to create your own composition! Just like authors write books and create original stories from their imaginations, composers write music and create original pieces. Why do you think a musician might choose to compose a piece of music?” Invite students to respond. Then share that music is a form of communication, and is often used to share a feeling or emotion, share stories or ideas, and/or support stories being told in other formats such as music playing in the background of a movie or TV show.

Composition in a B-A-G

Prepare two paper bags (prior to the start of class). One is labeled “Pitch” and the other is labeled “Rhythm.” Using the pitch printout provided, print and cut the lettered squares into individual pieces of paper that include the letters B, A, or G. There should be eight paper squares for each letter. Place them in the “Pitch Bag.” Then cut up the quarter notes, paired eighth notes, and quarter rests and place them in the “Rhythm Bag.”

Show students both bags and explain that the class will be composing a song by drawing pieces of paper out of the bag. Display four blank measures on the board with a 4/4 time signature:

Begin by having the first student draw a slip of paper from the rhythm bag and hold it up for the class to see. Draw the symbol on the first measure of the staff. For example, if a quarter rest is pulled from the bag, write it on the staff as follows:

If the rhythm symbol is a note, such as a quarter note, invite the next student to come to the front and draw a slip of paper from the pitch bag. Then, write the corresponding note value and pitch on the first measure of the staff. For example, if the next rhythm selected is a quarter note and the next student draws the pitch “A.” You would write a quarter note on the A space of the staff, next to the quarter rest:

If a student selects a pair of eighth notes, the next student will select a pitch for both notes. For example, if the third rhythm drawn is 2 eighth notes and the pitch is a “G”, you would right the next notes on the staff as a pair of G eighth notes:

If the next student chooses a quarter note next and the pitch is a “G”, write it next to the pair of eighth notes to complete the measure:

Students have now composed the first measure of their group song! After the first measure is completed, ask students to clap the rhythm. Then, as the teacher, play the first measure so students can hear the notes and rhythm together.

Continue selecting students to draw a rhythm and pitch from the bags to complete the four measure composition. After each measure is complete, clap the rhythm as a group and then play the new measure for students to hear the pitch and rhythm together. There should be four rhythm symbols drawn per measure with up to four pitches (if there are no rests).

Once the composition is complete, play through the full piece of music 2-3 times while students listen and reflect.

Reflection

Explain to students that the composition was created by a completely random selection of notes and rhythms. However, even random combinations can lead to interesting sounds, moods, and styles of music. Ask students, “What thoughts or reflections do you have about our class composition? What do you like/dislike? Does it sound like any other songs we have played? Could you imagine adding lyrics to this piece and turning it into a song? Why or why not?” Discuss in small groups or as a full class.

Sight-Reading

Play the following songs using these steps for sight-reading:

  • Step 1: “Read” through the piece of music, identifying which notes will be used.

  • Step 3: Silently “play” the song in “ready position” (without your mouth touching the instrument), practicing correct finger placement for each note.
  • Step 4: Play the song aloud.

1-10 Check-In

Ask students how they are feeling today. “Take a few moments to check-in with yourself and notice how you are feeling. Do you feel good? Bad? Excited? Nervous? Somewhere in the middle? Remember, there is no right or wrong response, as long as you are being truthful.”

Go around the room, asking students to share their number, from 1-10, responding to each student’s number with a neutral/appreciative acknowledgement of any number they choose.

Lesson Purpose

Tell students that today they will learn the difference between rhythm and beat and how to read some new music symbols.

Assess Prior Knowledge

Ask students, “Does anyone remember what the term ‘beat’ means in music?” Allow students to respond. Remind them that the beat is the pulse of the music and remains steady, just like a heartbeat. Then ask students, “What do you think the word ‘rhythm’ means in music?” Invite 2-3 students to respond.

",,,"

If You Can Hear My Voice

“Now it is time to warm up our bodies and voices so that we are prepared to focus, have fun, and make music together.”

Begin every class warm-up with the singing cue, “If you can hear my voice,_____________.” The phrase can be finished with any cue and can be sung on solfège scale degrees, “sol-do-do-do-do-do-do-sol,” or any simple melody of your choice. For example, you might sing, “If you can hear my voice, stand up.” Give them a few cues to get used to this method of listening and following directions. Teachers can use this or another attention-getter during transitions or moments when students need to focus and be attentive during instruction.

Sample cues:

“Stand up”

“Reach up tall”

“Stretch to your toes”

“Shoulders up, shoulders back, shoulders down”

“Wave hello”

“Twist back and forth”

“Sit down”

Flower/Candle Breathing

Explain that recorder players often include breathing exercises in their warm-up activities to help them practice breath control. Today’s technique is called Flower/Candle Breathing.

Hold one hand in a fist (as if holding a single flower stem) and the other hand with your pointer finger facing up (to represent a single candle). As you breathe in, hold the flower hand up to your nose, imagining you are smelling the flower; then breathe out, blowing the finger of the other hand as if blowing out a candle. Explain that the exhale should be long and slow air, just like they were playing a long note on the recorder. Practice this several times.

","

Notation Review

Display a blank staff on the board and ask students, “Raise your hand if you remember what this pattern of lines is called in music.” After students have responded, write the word, “staff” under the 5 lines. Then write a treble clef and ask if students remember the term for the symbol.

Next, write 4 whole notes in the spaces between the lines on the staff. Ask students, “What are the letter names that go with the notes in the spaces? What trick can we use to help us remember?” Write the letters F-A-C-E under the notes.

Repeat with the notes on the lines and their corresponding letter names, reminding students of the mnemonic device: Every Good Boy Does Fine.

Beat and Rhythm

“Earlier in the class, I asked you about the difference between rhythm and beat. Let’s begin by clapping a steady beat together.” Begin clapping a slow, steady beat and have students clap along. “Rest position!” Once students have stopped clapping, explain that just like our heart, the beat can sometimes be fast and at other times be slow. “Do you remember a time when your heart was beating really fast? How about when it was beating slowly?” Invite students to share a few examples. Then clap a fast, steady beat and ask students to clap along with you, without letting the tempo become faster or slower than the beat you established.

Next, explain that while the beat is the heart or pulse of the music and stays steady, rhythm is made up of the long and short sounds that can be measured by the beat. Show an example by asking a small group of students to clap a steady beat while you clap various rhythms over the beat. “Let’s play a few different rhythms together. I am going to clap a 4-beat rhythm pattern, and then I would like you to clap back as my echo.” Demonstrate an example to check for understanding, and then practice 6-8 various rhythm patterns using call-and-response.

Quarter Note

Explain that you can write rhythms using various notes and rests. Show students a quarter note symbol using either a laminated card, screen projection, or simply by writing it on the board. Explain that a quarter note is one beat, or one sound.

Notate 4 quarter notes in a row (using white board, projection, or printed sheet), and ask students how they think this rhythm might be played, using claps. Have them clap 4 times in unison.

Quarter Rest

“One of the most important things when playing music is understanding when you are supposed to be silent, or rest. If we were to play constantly without any gaps or silences, it would no longer be music, it would just be sound! In the same way that we have notes or sounds of various length, we also have rests of various length. Just like the quarter note has one beat, a quarter rest signals the musician to rest, or stay silent, for one beat.

Show students the symbol for a quarter rest on the board (or using projection, or a laminated printout with the symbol). Then display the pattern (below) and ask students to guess what the rhythm pattern would sound like when clapped. Ask for a student volunteer to clap the pattern first, then invite the full class to play, counting them in with a steady beat, “One, two, read-y, play.”

","

Instrument Distribution

Ask students to sit quietly in their chairs and place their hands folded on top of the desk. Distribute the student’s recorder and music folder by placing each on top of their desk (feel free to designate 2-3 student helpers to assist in passing out instruments and materials). Remind students to wait before touching or playing their instruments or folders until they have been instructed to do so.

Review First Note: B

Invite students to place their hand map on the desk in front of them for reference. Write or display 4 quarter notes on the B line of the staff and ask students, “Do you think you could play four quarter notes on B on your recorder? Ready position!” Check for correct finger placement in the ready position before cueing, “One, two, read-y, play.” Remind students to place the recorder gently on the top of their desks, hands in their lap so as not to be tempted to touch the instrument.

Be My Echo

Have students return to Rest position as you explain the next activity. Play a 4-beat rhythm pattern on a B on the recorder and then ask students to echo the rhythm they hear. Vary the rhythm patterns, playing a variety of long and short sounds that students will repeat on their instruments. Cue, “Ready position,” to have students pick up the recorder, place their hands on B, and wait for the first rhythm to be played by the teacher. Students will then play the rhythm back in response. Practice this activity with 8-10 different call and response rhythms, only playing on the B note.

","

Collect Materials

Have students return their recorders inside their case and collect all instruments and music folders. If students take the recorders home, instruct them to place them safely in their backpacks or desks. If the instruments stay in the classroom, designate a bin or other storage container to collect the recorders and music folders. Use student helpers to make this clean up process safe and efficient.

Reflection

Ask students, “What is the difference between rhythm and beat?” Invite students to discuss with a partner next to them and then share out 3-5 responses for the full class.

Recorder Wave — stand in “Musicians ready” position, lift your left hand up, lift your right hand, and shake both hands with palms open. As you do the movements, say, “Left” (holding up the left hand), “Right” (hold up the right hand), “Outta sight!” (shaking both hands in silent applause and then quickly placing them behind your back). Continue on to the bow:

One-Arm Bow — lift one arm up to the ceiling, fold forward bringing your arm down by your ankles, leave both arms down by your side and stand back up tall, returning to “Musicians ready” position.

Spaghetti Bow — lift one arm up toward the ceiling; as you fold forward, spiral your hand in a fancy gesture, as if spinning spaghetti noodles around your hand, and bring the arm across the waist. Then, stand back up, bringing your arm back to the side in “Musicians ready” position.

One-Leg Bow — step one leg out to the side and cross the other leg behind. Bend the standing leg and fold forward in a curtsy bringing either one arm in front of the chest or presenting both arms out wide to the side. Practice on both sides.

Finish with a group round of applause.

Lesson Purpose

Tell students that today they will learn their next note, an A! They will continue practicing articulation for clean sounds and various rhythm patterns using our quarter notes and rests.

Assess Prior Knowledge

Ask students, “What letter of the alphabet do we make with our tongue to articulate pitches when playing recorder?” Invite students to call out the response: the letter D.

",,,"

If You Can Hear My Voice

“Now it is time to warm up our bodies and voices so that we are prepared to focus, have fun, and make music together.”

Begin every class warm-up with the singing cue, “If you can hear my voice,_____________.” The phrase can be finished with any cue and can be sung on solfège scale degrees, “sol-do-do-do-do-do-do-sol,” or any simple melody of your choice. For example, you might sing, “If you can hear my voice, stand up.” Give them a few cues to get used to this method of listening and following directions. Teachers can use this or another attention-getter during transitions or moments when students need to focus and be attentive during instruction.

Sample cues:

“Stand up”

“Reach up tall”

“Stretch to your toes”

“Shoulders up, shoulders back, shoulders down”

“Wave hello”

“Twist back and forth”

“Sit down”

Tongue Twisters

“Musicians ready!” Have students repeat each tongue twister after you, always beginning with your voice first, then they repeat as a group. Then, challenge them to say it 3 times in a row.

Let them all practice at the same time and then ask if 3 volunteers would like to try it in front of the group. Then repeat with the next tongue twister, encouraging them to pronounce each sound clearly.

Tongue twister #1: “Don’t dilly dally.”

Tongue twister #2: “David doodles daily.”

Tongue twister #3: “Dirty dishes drip and drop.”

","

New Note: A

Begin by displaying a B (whole note) on the staff and playing a B on the recorder. Ask students, “What is the letter name for this note?” Invite students to call out in unison. Then ask them to listen carefully as you play a new note, “See if you can tell if the note sounds higher or lower than the B, and if you can see my fingers changing position.” Play a B first, then switch to an A. Invite students to raise their hand if they think the new note is higher/lower.

Next, display a B (whole note) on the staff and ask, “If the new note sounds lower, do you think that it will be written on a higher or lower line on the staff? Lower! As notes get lower in pitch, they are written lower on the staff. And as notes get higher in pitch, they are written higher on the staff.”

Write the word “pitch” on the board and ask students to say the term aloud. Explain that pitch simply means how high or low a note sounds in music.

“To play this new note, notice that the 3rd finger on my left hand is going to cover the second hole on the front of the recorder.” Demonstrate switching from note B to A.

Instrument Distribution

Ask students to sit quietly in their chairs and place their hands folded on top of the desk. Distribute the student’s recorder and music folder by placing each on top of their desk (feel free to designate 2-3 student helpers to assist in passing out instruments and materials). Remind students to wait before touching or playing their instruments or folders until they have been instructed to do so.

Note A

Invite students to place their hand map on the desk in front of them for reference. Model the finger position to play note A and ask all students to prepare their finger position in the ready position. Ask students to check that their fingers are fully covering each hole, explaining that the pitch will sound different if the hole is not completely covered. Then cue them to play note A, holding for 15-30 seconds while the teacher rotates through the room, correcting finger positions or slow breathing, as needed.

Next, give students 30-60 seconds to practice switching between notes A and B, reminding them of their tongue articulation so they can clearly separate each pitch from the other. This will sound chaotic with everyone playing the notes at different times; however, it is important to build in this free time for exploration so that students feel comfortable practicing independently.

Rhythms on A

Ask students to look at the “Rhythms on A” sheet music from their music folder or display a copy of the music on the board or projection screen. Cue them to play each line of rhythms on their recorder, in unison. (If students need additional rhythm practice when site-reading the music, clap the rhythms first before playing on the instrument).

If students take the recorders home, instruct them to place them safely in their backpacks or desks. If the instruments stay in the classroom, designate a bin or other storage container to collect the recorders and music folders. Use student helpers to make this clean up process safe and efficient.

Reflection

Ask students, “Is the A note higher or lower than the B note?” Invite students to answer with a thumbs up for higher or a thumbs down for lower. Then ask, “Is the A note on a line or in a space? What about the B note?”

Lesson Purpose

Assess Prior Knowledge

Remind students of the staff and note names using the following diagram:

Ask students, “How do we remember the note names for notes that are placed in the spaces between the line? (F-A-C-E) How do we remember the note names for notes placed on the lines? (Every Good Boy Does Fine) Where are the two E notes on the staff?” Ask a student to come up to the board and point to the low E and high E on the staff. Then play the low E on the recorder and ask students if they think this note will be the low E or high E. (Low E, on the bottom line).

If You Can Hear My Voice (Student-Led)

“Now it is time to warm up our bodies and voices so that we are prepared to focus, have fun, and make music together.”

Invite a student from the class to lead the warm-up using the singing cue, “If you can hear my voice, _____________.” The phrase can be finished with any cue and can be sung on solfège scale degrees, “sol-do-do-do-do-do-do-sol,” or any simple melody of your choice. You can select a new student leader for each class. As the student sings the warm-up cues, you as the teacher should follow along with the rest of the class.

Sample cues:

“Stand up”

“Reach up tall”

“Stretch to your toes”

“Shoulders up, shoulders back, shoulders down”

“Wave hello”

“Twist back and forth”

“Sit down”

Instrument Distribution

Ask students to sit quietly in their chairs and place their hands folded on top of the desk. Distribute the student’s recorder and music folder by placing each on top of their desk (feel free to designate 2-3 student helpers to assist in passing out instruments and materials). Remind students to wait before touching or playing their instruments or folders until they have been instructed to do so.

Warm-Up on Low D and G

Begin by playing the Warm-Ups on Low D and G, encouraging students to play each line with accuracy in rhythm and pitch.

New Note: E

“Our seventh note is an E. I am going to play the note, and you tell me with your thumbs if the note sounds higher or lower than the low D we learned in the previous class. Here is the low D (play a low D) and here is an E (play an E note). Is the E higher or lower?” Invite students to show higher or lower with their thumbs. “The E is higher than the low D and is placed on the bottom line of the staff.” Label the E note and add to the staff with the previously learned notes (highlighting that the note is above the low D, but below the G):

Explain that to play the E on your recorder, you will cover the top 5 holes on the front of the instrument while your thumb covers the back hole. To make this low sound without squeaking, remind students to use slow air.

Ask students, “How is this finger placement different from the placement for a low D?” Show students the finger placement for a low D, then switch to an E, lifting the fourth finger on the right hand. Then have students alternate between playing a low D and E to practice lifting and lowering the fourth finger.

Warm-Ups on E

Play Warm-Ups on E to practice the new note using various rhythms. Then play Warm-Ups on D and E to practice switching between the two notes.

Review Ode to Joy

Practice the song 2-3 times all the way through, ensuring all students are playing the rhythm and notes with accuracy. Encourage students to play with slow air, be sure to cover the finger holes completely, and listen to the other musicians to help everyone play together as one.

Review When the Saints Go Marching In

Practice the song 2-3 times all the way through, ensuring all students are playing the rhythm and notes with accuracy. Encourage students to play with slow air, be sure to cover the finger holes completely, and listen to the other musicians to help everyone play together as one.

If students take the recorders home, instruct them to place them safely in their backpacks or desks. If the instruments stay in the classroom, designate a bin or other storage container to collect the recorders and music folders. Use student helpers to make this clean up process safe and efficient.

Reflection

“Now you will have a turn to lead the game ‘Higher/Lower’.” Invite a student to come to the board and select one of the 7 notes learned thus far and write the letter name on the board. The teacher will then play this note on the recorder. Ask the student to then write the letter name of a second note on the board. The teacher will play the second note. Ask students to listen to the two different notes and show a thumbs up/down if they think the second note is higher in pitch (thumbs up) or lower in pitch (thumbs down). Then point to both notes on the music staff to confirm the correct answer and show that any note that is higher in pitch than another note will be on a higher line or space on the staff.

Assess Prior Knowledge

If You Can Hear My Voice

“Now it is time to warm up our bodies and voices so that we are prepared to focus, have fun, and make music together.”

Begin every class warm-up with the singing cue, “If you can hear my voice,_____________.” The phrase can be finished with any cue and can be sung on solfège scale degrees, “sol-do-do-do-do-do-do-sol,” or any simple melody of your choice. For example, you might sing, “If you can hear my voice, stand up.” Give them a few cues to get used to this method of listening and following directions. Teachers can use this or another attention-getter during transitions or moments when students need to focus and be attentive during instruction.

Sample cues:

“Stand up”

“Reach up tall”

“Stretch to your toes”

“Shoulders up, shoulders back, shoulders down”

“Wave hello”

“Twist back and forth”

“Sit down”

Flower/Candle Breathing

Explain that recorder players often include breathing exercises in their warm-up activities to help them practice breath control. Today’s technique is called Flower/Candle Breathing.

Hold one hand in a fist (as if holding a single flower stem) and the other hand with your pointer finger facing up (to represent a single candle). As you breathe in, hold the flower hand up to your nose, imagining you are smelling the flower; then breathe out, blowing the finger of the other hand as if blowing out a candle. Explain that the exhale should be long and slow air, just like they were playing a long note on the recorder. Practice this several times.

Tongue Twisters

“Musicians ready!” Have students repeat each tongue twister after you, always beginning with your voice first, then they repeat as a group. Then, challenge them to say it 3 times in a row.

Let them all practice at the same time and then ask if 3 volunteers would like to try it in front of the group. Then repeat with the next tongue twister, encouraging them to pronounce each sound clearly.

Tongue twister #1: “Does the dog do downward dog?”

Tongue twister #2: “Do dewdrops drop dew?”

Tongue twister #3: “Daisy and Daniel dropped the donuts!”

","

Sheet Music Symbol Identification

Distribute the blank sheet music worksheet (included) and a pencil to each student. “Let’s begin by labeling the parts we have already learned. Raise your hand if you can identify a symbol on this sheet music that you recognize.” Invite students to label the following elements: staff, treble clef, quarter note and quarter rest.

“Do you notice any other symbols or markings on this music that we haven’t learned yet?” Explain that the small, vertical lines on the staff are called “bar lines” and break up the music into “measures.” Write “bar line” and “measure” on the board. Then ask students to label these on the worksheet.

Next, show students the 4/4 time signature on the left side of each line of music, next to the treble clef. Explain that this is called a time signature (write this term on the board) and tells the musician how many beats there are in each measure. “The most common time signature is 4/4, like we see on this music. This means that there are 4 beats per measure (point to the top number 4), and each beat is a quarter note (point to the bottom number 4). So every 4 beats, you will see a barline to indicate the end of the measure.

“There is one final symbol on this worksheet that we have not learned yet. Can anyone spot it?” Show them the repeat symbol at the end of each line. “This is called a ‘repeat sign’ and tells the musician to repeat the whole section of music again. If you see a double line at the end of the staff (without the two dots) this means the end of the song. But if there are two dots (reference on the displayed music), this tells you to repeat all of the music from the beginning.”

Have students label the top and bottom of the time signature as well as the repeat symbol. This worksheet can be used as a reference to remember the sheet music symbols and should be stored in the student’s music folder.

Remind students to wait before touching or playing their instruments or folders until they have been instructed to do so.

nvite students to place their hand map on the desk in front of them for reference. Write or display 4 quarter notes on the B line of the staff and ask students, “Do you think you can play four quarter notes on B on your recorder? Ready position!” Check for correct finger position in the ready position before cueing, “One, two, read-y, play.”

Articulation

Have students return to Rest position. Then ask, “Did you notice how the sounds of each note blended together as we all played? So it almost sounded like one long B sound? In order to create clear, distinct tones on the recorder, we must learn ‘articulation’.” Ask students to repeat the word “articulation,” and write it on the board. Explain that this is a word to describe how to make clean, clear sounds for each note by using your tongue.

Remind them of the tongue twisters from the warm-up and ask, “Does anyone remember what letter of the alphabet we used for our tongue twister warm-up? The letter D! This is because the position of your tongue when making a ‘D’ sound is the same position when making clean, crisp sounds on your recorder instrument. When playing the recorder, your tongue will hit the back of your teeth, just as if you were saying the letter ‘D,’ so your tongue should not be touching the mouthpiece itself. Let’s practice the four quarter notes again, and see if you can use your tongue to make those notes crisp and clean. Listen first to my example, and then I will cue you to come into ‘Ready position’.”

Demonstrate the difference between four slurred quarter notes on B and four separated notes using tongue articulation. Then cue students to come to Ready position and count them in to play, using their tongue to make four clear sounds, “One, two, read-y, play!”

Ask students to look at the “Rhythms on B” sheet music from their music folder or display a copy of the music on the board or projection screen. Clap each rhythm for the students first, then count them in to play each line of rhythms on their recorder, in unison.

Go around the room, asking students to share their number, from 1-10, responding to each student’s number with a neutral/appreciative acknowledgement of any number they choose.

Lesson Purpose

Tell students that today they will play their new compositions as a group and compose their own, individual melody line using all the notes they have learned so far.

Assess Prior Knowledge

Ask students, “What is a melody in music?” Invite 3-5 students to share their response. Then explain that a melody is a series of musical notes in a piece of music. The melody is often the most memorable part of a piece of music and the “catchy” part that we often sing or hum along to.

Hum the melodies of the songs below, 3 notes at a time. Ask students to guess the song, adding more notes as needed until they can name the tune.

Invite a student from the class to lead the warm-up using the singing cue, “If you can hear my voice, _____________.” The phrase can be finished with any cue and can be sung on solfège scale degrees, “sol-do-do-do-do-do-do-sol,” or any simple melody of your choice. You can select a new student leader for each class. As the student sings the warm-up cues, you as the teacher should follow along with the rest of the class.

Sample cues:

“Stand up”

“Reach up tall”

“Stretch to your toes”

“Shoulders up, shoulders back, shoulders down”

Instrument Distribution

Ask students to sit quietly in their chairs and place their hands folded on top of the desk. Distribute the student’s recorder and music folder by placing each on top of their desk (feel free to designate 2-3 student helpers to assist in passing out instruments and materials). Remind students to wait before touching or playing their instruments or folders until they have been instructed to do so.

Warm-Up

Play through the piece of music created in the “Composition in a B-A-G” class 2-3 times. Practice rhythms or transitions between notes as needed until the full class can play successfully together as a group.

Then invite 3 students to share their roll-the-dice compositions from the previous class. One student at a time, display the music on the board or projector and have students sight-read the 4 measures. Then continue on to the next student.

Compose a Melody

Now students will have the opportunity to compose their own melody line using the notes learned in class thus far. Begin by displaying a staff with the notes they have previously learned:

Ask students to play each note, one at a time, in unison. Check for correct finger placement and pitch, reviewing notes as needed.

Next, distribute the melody composition worksheet and a pencil to each student. Ask them to explore various note combinations on their recorder until they decide on a series of notes to record on the staff. Using only whole notes, record the 8 notes in the squares provided, then place the notes in sequence on the music staff.

Once all students have completed their 8-note melody line, invite 3-5 students to “perform” their melody for the class. After a student plays through their piece, the full class can sight-read the piece together and play it as a group.

Continue on to the bow:

One-Leg Bow — step one leg out to the side and cross the other leg behind. Bend the standing leg and fold forward in a curtsy bringing either one arm in front of the chest or presenting both arms out wide to the side. Practice on both sides.

Review the song, “Duke’s Place,” using the following steps:

  1. Clap the rhythm of the full song as a group.
  2. Play the song on the recorder, emphasizing correct notes and rhythm.
  3. Repeat and practice 2-3 times.

Tied Notes

“Now we will learn another symbol used in music called ‘a tie.’ Just like a string can tie two things together, a music tie connects two notes together.” Draw two tied B notes, explaining that the curved line connects the two notes together. “The tie connects two notes of the same pitch, such as two B’s or two C’s. Only the first note is played and then it is held for the length of both notes together.” Show the following examples on the board and ask students how many beats each pair of tied notes represents.

When the Saints Go Marching In

“Now let’s look at a song that includes dotted half notes and tied notes.” Distribute or display the music for “When the Saints Go Marching In.” Begin by asking students to raise their hand if they can point to a dotted note or pair of tied notes in the music. Then ask the students how many beats the note(s) represent(s). For example, in the second and third measure of the song, there is a whole note tied to a quarter note. With a whole note representing 4 beats and a quarter note representing 1 beat, the tied notes are held for a total of 5 beats. Think 4 + 1 = 5.

After identifying and reviewing the dotted and tied notes, pass out pencils and ask students to write the counts above each note of the song. This will help students stay on the correct count and play the rhythm in unison. Then play through the song, one measure at a time, counting the measures as the students play.

Toy vs. Tools

“Instruments can be incredibly fun to play but they also require a lot of control of your body and listening skills. While the recorder may look like a plastic toy, it is actually a very special tool that is intended to be used in specific ways that I will demonstrate. If at any point in our classes together I see that you are using the recorder as a toy instead of a tool, it will show me that you are not ready to use the instrument that day, and I will ask you to practice without the instrument for that class.

We will now distribute your recorder instrument and give you an opportunity to show that you are prepared to follow directions. Please place your hands folded, on top of your desk, and do not touch the instrument or your music folder until you have been instructed to do so.”

Instrument Distribution

Ask students to sit quietly in their chairs and place their hands folded on top of the desk. Distribute a recorder to each student, along with their music folder and place both on top of the desk (feel free to designate 2-3 student helpers to assist in passing out instruments and materials). Remind students to wait before touching or playing their instruments or folders until they have been instructed to do so.

Rest, Ready, and Play Positions

Explain to students that in addition to “Musicians ready,’ you have some additional cues for when they are playing their instruments. Teach and practice the three positions you will use for the recorder: rest, ready, and play position.

Rest position is where you place the recorder in your lap or on your desk. This position is used when you need students to listen to instructions and you should not hear any playing of instruments.

Ready position is when you place your hands on the recorder, left over right, and bring the instrument in front of your mouth, ready to play. Like rest position, you should not hear any sound or playing of instruments in ready position.

Play position is when you gently blow into the mouthpiece to play a note on the recorder. You are seated with a tall back, feet uncrossed and flat on the floor, sitting toward the edge of your seat.

Practice rest and ready position until all students respond with consistency and accuracy. There should be no sound coming from the recorder at this time. Then, with everyone seated in rest position, explain that when you say, “Play position,” students may pick up their instrument and freely blow into their recorder, practicing their slow breath and placing their hands left on top of right. “While you are playing, you will need to keep your eyes on me so you can see the cue to stop playing.” Demonstrate the conductor’s hand gesture to stop playing by holding up your open hand and wrapping it into a closed fist. Tell students that during this free play, they can experiment with their breathing, finger placement, etc. in any way they choose, as long as the playing stays at a medium-to-low volume (using slow air).

Cue, “Ready position,” and wait for all students to respond quietly, getting their instrument into the proper position for play. Then cue, “Play position,” and allow them 20-30 seconds to freely explore playing their recorder. Cue them to stop with the conductor’s hand gesture and ask students to return to “Rest position.” Remind students to place the recorder gently on the top of their desks, hands in lap so as not to be tempted to touch the instrument.

Simon Says

“A lot of our success this year is going to require careful listening and following directions. We are going to play a game of Simon Says to help you practice some of our cues together.”

Explain the rules of the game, “I am going to call out different directions that I would like you to follow. However, I only want you to follow the directions if you first hear me say, ‘Simon Says.’ If you don’t hear those words, continue doing what you were doing in the previous direction. For example, if you hear me say, ‘Simon says raise your right hand,’ you should all raise your right hand. But if my next instruction is, ‘Clap your hands three times,’ you should keep reaching your right hand up to the sky, because I didn’t say, ‘Simon Says’.”

Model and practice 1-2 rounds until all students are clear on how to play the game.

Directions should help them identify their right and left hands, play the recorder and stop playing on cue, etc. See the list below for suggested cues:

  2. Wiggle your fingers

  4. Play a quiet note on the recorder for a count of 3 and then return to rest position
  5. Raise your right hand above your head

For example, if a student responds, “Yes, I play the piano.” Ask the whole class, “Does anyone else play the piano? Raise a silent hand if you also play the piano.”

Musicians Ready!

Explain to students that during music class, there will be many times when the class will be making music and you will need to get their attention. “When I call out ‘Musicians ready!’, that is your cue to either...

Stand tall, feet together, knees pulled up straight, arms down by your sides (out of pockets or shirt sleeves) mouths closed. OR sit tall in your seat, feet flat on the ground, hands resting on top of desk. Head is lifted, shoulders down, eyes open, mouth closed. Head and eyes should be facing the teacher.”

Begin in the seated position at their tables or desks and have students practice the posture all together: correct any student’s position as needed. Then have students quietly stand up, push in their chairs, and practice the standing version.

Next, tell students that you are going to practice each version a few times to make sure they have it. When you say, “Silly sounds!” the students can move their bodies and talk in a silly way. Model this so students keep hands and bodies from touching or bothering anybody else. When they hear you say, “Musicians ready!” they should immediately stop their movement and noise, and freeze in the seated or standing position (depending on the activity). Tell students you will be using this phrase, “Musicians ready!” at the start and during each activity, so that they are ready to listen and learn.

Practice this skill 3-5 times until all students respond consistently with accuracy. Ask students to choose a partner, then demonstrate together that they can do “Musicians ready!” position. As the group calls out, “Musicians ready!” one pair at a time demonstrates.

Select four students to come to the front of the room and explain that the next song will help you to learn their names while keeping a steady beat. “A steady beat is like the heartbeat of the song, it remains even and steady, just like our own heartbeat.” Begin clapping a slow, steady beat and ask students to clap and sing along with you as they begin to pick up the pattern of the song.

If You Can Hear My Voice

“Now it is time to warm up our bodies and voices so that we are prepared to focus, have fun, and make music together.”

Begin every class warm-up with the singing cue, “If you can hear my voice,_____________.” The phrase can be finished with any cue and can be sung on solfège scale degrees, “sol-do-do-do-do-do-do-sol,” or any simple melody of your choice.

For example, you might sing, “If you can hear my voice, stand up.” Give them a few cues to get used to this method of listening and following directions. Teachers can use this or another attention-getter during transitions or moments when students need to focus and be attentive during instruction.

Sample cues:

“Stand up”

“Reach up tall”

“Stretch to your toes”

“Shoulders up, shoulders back, shoulders down”

“Wave hello”

“Twist back and forth”

“Sit down”

Introduction to the Recorder

Begin by showing students a recorder instrument (explain that they will receive their own instrument in the third class, once they have learned proper breathing techniques and hand placement). Pass the recorder around the class, allowing students to hold the instrument, without touching it to their mouth or blowing through it.

Explain that in music, instruments fall into different categories, or “families.” The four most common families of instruments are woodwinds, brass, strings, and percussion. Ask students, “Does anyone remember what instrument family the recorder is a part of?” It is in the woodwinds family! This means that we use “wind” or air to make sounds on the instrument and historically these instruments were all made of wood. Nowadays, we often see woodwinds made from metal, plastic, wood, or some combination of the three. Ask, “Does anyone know any other instruments that are part of the woodwind family?” After a few suggestions from students, share that flutes, clarinets, saxophones, oboes, and bassoons are also part of this family.

Show students the parts of the recorder including the head joint (or mouthpiece), the body, and the foot. Explain that there are seven holes on the front of the instrument and one hole on the back. In order to make different-sounding notes, your fingers will cover different combinations of holes while blowing through the mouthpiece.

Breathing Air Hockey

Perhaps the most important skill in playing the recorder is learning how to use your breath. Begin with a fun activity to practice breath control using either a ping pong ball or ball of paper.

Have students place a ping pong ball (or balled-up piece of paper) at the edge of their table or desk and see if they can blow the ball from one side of the desk to the other without using their hands and without the ball falling off the table top.

Begin first by using slow air and notice what happens to the ball. Then try again blowing fast air and notice how that changes the accuracy and success of the game.

Ask, “When playing the recorder, do you think we will use fast air or slow air?” Explain that slow air will give us more control and accuracy in the notes we are playing, just like in the ball activity.

",,"

Collect all materials and ask students to return to a seated position at their desk. “Musicians ready!”

Ask students, “What kind of air do we use when playing the recorder?” Invite 2-3 students to respond. Then ask, “There is one hole on the back of the instrument, but does anyone remember how many holes are on the front of the recorder? Show me by holding up your fingers how many holes you think there are on the front side.”

For the first class, explain to students that you will end every class with a phrase and custom bow to celebrate their great effort, focus, and participation. Explain that performers, including musicians, take a bow to thank their audience for watching and listening to them perform and it is something we will practice each class. Standing next to their desks, demonstrate, teach, and practice the recorder wave and three bows that they can choose from:

Recorder Wave — stand in “Musicians ready” position, lift your left hand up, lift your right hand, and shake both hands with palms open. As you do the movements, say, “Left” (holding up the left hand), “Right” (hold up the right hand), “Outta sight!” (shaking both hands in silent applause and then quickly placing them behind your back). Continue on to the the bow choices below:

One-Arm Bow — lift one arm up to the ceiling, fold forward bringing your arm down by your ankles, leave both arms down by your side and stand back up tall, returning to “Musicians ready” position.

Spaghetti Bow — lift one arm up toward the ceiling; as you fold forward, spiral your hand in a fancy gesture, as if spinning spaghetti noodles around your hand, and bring the arm across the waist. Then, stand back up, bringing your arm back to the side in “Musicians ready” position.

One-Leg Bow — step one leg out to the side and cross the other leg behind. Bend the standing leg and fold forward in a curtsy bringing either one arm in front of the chest or presenting both arms out wide to the side. Practice on both sides.

Finish with a group round of applause.

Rhythm Composition

Distribute the “Compose Your Own Rhythm” worksheet and a pair of scissors and a glue stick to each student. Explain that students will use the symbols on the right side of the page to create their own sequence of notes and rests to compose an original rhythm. Instruct students to begin by cutting out the notes and rest symbols in the squares on the right-hand side of the worksheet. There should be ten squares in total, in varying sizes depending on the number of beats they represent.

Once all squares have been cut out, students can then arrange the notes and rests on the four measures on the left-hand side of the worksheet. Explain to students that they are working in 4/4 time so there must be a total of 4 beats in each measure. They will know the measure is complete when all four squares are covered by the cut-out notation symbols. Ask students to glue their squares onto the measures and return the scissors and glue when they have completed the activity. Then, proceed to distribute the recorders.

Instrument Distribution

Ask students to sit quietly in their chairs and place their hands folded on top of the desk. Distribute the student’s recorder and music folder by placing each on top of their desk (feel free to designate 2-3 student helpers to assist in passing out instruments and materials). Remind students to wait before touching or playing their instruments or folders until they have been instructed to do so.

Rhythm Play

Invite a student to share his/her/their composition in front of the class using a dot cam or other form of display. Ask the students to select a pitch (high D, C, B, A, G, E, or low D) and then lead the class through the 4 measures of rhythm on the selected pitch. Play through 2-3 times until everyone is accurately playing in unison.

Continue this exercise with new student rhythms each time, allowing time for 4-6 students to share.

",,"

Collect Materials

Have students return their recorders inside their case and collect all instruments and music folders. If students take the recorders home, instruct them to place them safely in their backpacks or desks. If the instruments stay in the classroom, designate a bin or other storage container to collect the recorders and music folders. Use student helpers to make this clean up process safe and efficient.

Reflection

Ask students to share about their process and experience composing their rhythm line. “How did you decide where to place each symbol? What did you enjoy about the activity? What did you find challenging?” Invite students to discuss as a group.

Music Composition

Distribute the previous melody and rhythm worksheets to each students along with the “Music Composition” worksheet and a pencil. Begin by explaining that the first step to completing the compositions will be to add in our melody line to the rhythm worksheet. “You will notice that in each box on your rhythm worksheet that contains a note, there is a small, blank box. These smaller boxes are where you will write the letter for each note in your melody. Begin with the first measure of your rhythm and identify where you play your first note. Then, referencing your melody line, write the letter of the first pitch of your melody in the small box. For example, if the first note in your melody is a C, write the letter “C” in the first note box on your rhythm measures. Continue adding each note to the small squares until you have completed the four measures of music.” It is recommended to guide students through this activity, one note at a time, to ensure all students feel successful combining their pitch with the rhythm outline. Display an example and model the instructions as you give them. (See visual example below)

After all students have written in their note values, it is time to begin transcribing their composition onto the staff. Using the “Music Composition” worksheet as a guide, begin by explaining the “stem rule” so students understand when the stem of a note should face up or down.

“If the notehead (circle part) of your note falls on the middle line of the staff or above, you always draw the stem (or line) facing down on the left-hand side. If the notehead falls below the middle line, the stem will extend up from the notehead on the right-hand side. So you will want to pay close attention as you begin to write in your notes, that the stems are facing the right direction.”

Next, model for students how to take each measure on the worksheet and transfer to the staff. “Looking at your staff, point to the first measure. This is where you will notate the first measure of notes and/or rests.” Model notating the first measure with your example:

What is Stage Fright?

  2. Sing the note names while clapping the rhythm

If You Can Hear My Voice

“Now it is time to warm up our bodies and voices so that we are prepared to focus, have fun, and make music together.”

“The next note you will learn is a symbol you have already seen before!” Display the music staff with the 8 whole notes used in the Week 4 lesson:

Explain that when you see a note that is open in the middle and does not include a stem, (or line) extending from the note head, it is a whole note. 1-10 Check-In

Ask students how they are feeling today. “Take a few moments to check-in with yourself and notice how you are feeling. Do you feel good? Bad? Excited? Nervous? Somewhere in the middle? Remember, there is no right or wrong response, as long as you are being truthful.”

Go around the room, asking students to share their number, from 1-10, responding to each student’s number with a neutral/appreciative acknowledgement of any number they choose.

Lesson Purpose

Tell students that today they will learn the note C on the recorder and a song that uses all four notes learned so far. “There are so many songs you can play – just using these four notes!”

Assess Prior Knowledge

Ask students, “Can you figure out what song I am clapping?” Then clap the rhythm to “Mary Had a Little Lamb.” Ask students to raise their hand if they can guess the song. After selecting a student and getting the correct response, ask all students to clap the rhythm of the song together.

",,,"

If You Can Hear My Voice

“Now it is time to warm up our bodies and voices so that we are prepared to focus, have fun, and make music together.”

Begin every class warm-up with the singing cue, “If you can hear my voice,_____________.” The phrase can be finished with any cue and can be sung on solfège scale degrees, “sol-do-do-do-do-do-do-sol,” or any simple melody of your choice. For example, you might sing, “If you can hear my voice, stand up.” Give them a few cues to get used to this method of listening and following directions. Teachers can use this or another attention-getter during transitions or moments when students need to focus and be attentive during instruction.

Sample cues:

“Stand up”

“Reach up tall”

“Stretch to your toes”

“Shoulders up, shoulders back, shoulders down”

“Wave hello”

“Twist back and forth”

“Sit down”

New Note: C

“Our fourth note is a C. I am going to play the note, and you tell me with your thumbs if the note sounds higher or lower than the other three notes we have learned so far.” Play the note C and allow students to show higher or lower with their thumbs. If most students guessed incorrectly, play the notes B, A, and G first, followed by the C. “The C is higher than the previous three notes and is placed higher on the staff. Using the tool F-A-C-E, ask students to guess where on the staff we should place the C note. Tell them, “Like A, C is in a space, not on a line of the staff.”

This note is played by covering the thumb hole in the back and the second hole on the front using your second finger on your left hand. Be sure to lift your 1 and 3 fingers to make a clear sound. Demonstrate the finger position and play the note C.

Instrument Distribution

Ask students to sit quietly in their chairs and place their hands folded on top of the desk. Distribute the student’s recorder and music folder by placing each on top of their desk (feel free to designate 2-3 student helpers to assist in passing out instruments and materials). Remind students to wait before touching or playing their instruments or folders until they have been instructed to do so.

Note C

Invite students to place their hand map on the desk in front of them for reference. Model the finger position to play note C and ask all students to prepare their finger position in the ready position. Then, cue them to play note C, holding for 15-30 seconds while the teacher rotates through the room, correcting finger positions or slow breathing, as needed.

Next, give students 30-60 seconds to practice switching between notes C, B, A, and G, reminding them of their tongue articulation so they can make clearly separate each pitch from the other. This will sound chaotic with everyone playing the notes at different times; however, it is important to build in this free time for exploration so that students feel comfortable practicing independently.

Rhythms on C

Ask students to look at the “Rhythms on C” sheet music from their music folder or display a copy of the music on the board or projection screen. Practice each line on the sheet or ask for students to pick a line of rhythms to play as a class, in unison.

Song Review

Play the following songs as a group, practicing parts as necessary if students need additional support. Encourage students to play with slow air, be sure to cover the finger holes completely, and listen to the other musicians to help everyone play together as one.

  • “Hot Cross Buns”
  • “Mary Had a Little Lamb”
  • “Au Clair de la Lune”

Juba

Have students return to Rest position, recorders on top of the desk, hands in lap. Display the sheet music for “Juba” and explain that this song comes from African music and dance traditions and was widely known during the period of slavery in the United States.

  • Play the song first for students, asking them to follow along on their sheet music using their finger.
  • Then, have the class sing the song as a group using call and response.
  • Next, have students sing the note names and clap the rhythm.
  • Finally, have them play the song on the recorder, emphasizing correct notes and rhythm.
  • Repeat and practice 2-3 times.
",,"

Collect Materials

Have students return their recorders inside their case and collect all instruments and music folders. If students take the recorders home, instruct them to place them safely in their backpacks or desks. If the instruments stay in the classroom, designate a bin or other storage container to collect the recorders and music folders. Use student helpers to make this clean up process safe and efficient.

Reflection

Ask students, “What is your favorite song to play that you have learned in class?” Invite 3-5 students to respond, encouraging the rest of the students to “silent shake” in agreement if they liked similar things being shared.

Recorder Wave — stand in “Musicians ready” position, lift your left hand up, lift your right hand, and shake both hands with palms open. As you do the movements, say, “Left” (holding up the left hand), “Right” (hold up the right hand), “Outta sight!” (shaking both hands in silent applause and then quickly placing them behind your back). Continue on to the bow:

One-Arm Bow — lift one arm up to the ceiling, fold forward bringing your arm down by your ankles, leave both arms down by your side and stand back up tall, returning to “Musicians ready” position.

Spaghetti Bow — lift one arm up toward the ceiling; as you fold forward, spiral your hand in a fancy gesture, as if spinning spaghetti noodles around your hand, and bring the arm across the waist. Then, stand back up, bringing your arm back to the side in “Musicians ready” position.

One-Leg Bow — step one leg out to the side and cross the other leg behind. Bend the standing leg and fold forward in a curtsy bringing either one arm in front of the chest or presenting both arms out wide to the side. Practice on both sides.

Finish with a group round of applause.
